<header>Verse 18] The Commentary by the Illustrious Teacher Abhinavagupta. 223</header>

<meta>continues from previous page: She, the power of reflection, has for her sphere separate objects of consciousness,</meta>

->**and is named as knowledge, intention, determination, and so forth.**<- [Verse 18]

<term>Māyā</term> <gloss>illusion</gloss> is defined as an appearance that is inconsistent with reality <note>original: "anupapannam avabhāsanaṃ"</note>. Consequently, everything that appears as separate from the light of consciousness is a product of <term>Māyā</term>. In that context, the very freedom of the principle of consciousness is called the <term>Māyā-śakti</term> <gloss>the power of illusion</gloss>. By that power, the object of consciousness becomes separated from the subject and from other objects. That very consciousness, which consists of <term>pratyavamarśa</term> <gloss>reflective awareness</gloss> and is the nature of the <term>Parā-vāk</term> <gloss>Supreme Speech</gloss>, is said to be "knowledge," "intention," and "determination" when its sphere—its place of rest—is the object of consciousness made separate by the <term>Māyā-śakti</term> <note>that is, separate from the knower and from other objects through the group of senses</note>. The term "and so forth" includes doubt, memory, and other states. To explain: that which is grasped through the clear external senses—

---

<note>399. This is the gist of the verse: Through the <term>Māyā-śakti</term> of the Supreme Lord, who is the essence of Light, the universe—which is actually His own self—is made to appear as separate. Therefore, that same consciousness is "knowledge" <term>jñāna</term> when it is direct perception. Memory, intention, and determination of that same separate appearance are also just consciousness, even when taking the form of the activities of the mind and intellect.</note>
<note>400. This shows the grammatical resolution of the term "freedom within <term>Māyā</term>."</note>
<note>401. Regarding "from the knower": The Self is indeed the all-pervading Supreme Lord. However, through the <term>Māyā-śakti</term>, He becomes a limited subject <term>grāhaka</term> <gloss>grasper</gloss> due to contraction. Similarly, the power of reflection also becomes contracted by the influence of objects that have been limited by the <term>Māyā-śakti</term>. In this state, it is called "knowledge," "memory," and so on. But the point is that these are not separate principles other than the power of reflection itself; they are merely different names.</note>
<note>402. This explains the phrase "separate objects of consciousness" by adopting the view of repeated manifestation.</note>

<summary>This page concludes Verse 18, explaining that Maya is the Lord's power to make the world appear separate from Himself. It identifies various mental states like knowledge and intention as modes of the single power of reflection.</summary>
<keywords>Maya, Maya-shakti, Paravak, Pratyavamarsha, knowledge, intention, determination, consciousness, Abhinavagupta</keywords>

Meditation on the dawn and other times as the head and limbs of the sacrificial horse, because the horse is the primary element in the <term>Ashvamedha</term> <gloss>horse sacrifice</gloss> ... 8

Meditation on the day and other symbols within the ritual vessels called <term>Mahiman</term> <gloss>greatness cups</gloss> ... 11

A description of the creation of the universe up to the element of water; this establishes the theory that the effect exists within the cause <note>original: "satkaryavada"</note> while refuting the theory that the effect is non-existent before creation; this serves to praise the birth of the sacrificial fire ... 13

Meditation on the eastern direction and other quarters as the head and limbs of the sacrificial Fire ... 23

Definition of the terms <term>Ashva</term> <gloss>horse</gloss> and <term>Ashvamedha</term> <gloss>horse sacrifice</gloss>; a specific injunction for the meditation on the horse sacrifice, showing the result as attaining the state of <term>Hiranyagarbha</term> <gloss>the Golden Embryo or Cosmic Soul</gloss>, who is Death ... 28

The relationship between the previous and subsequent sections; after describing the results of knowledge and ritual, this section defines the nature of <term>Prana</term> <gloss>the vital force</gloss> which liberates one from both; an allegorical story of the speech and other faculties of <term>Prajapati</term> <gloss>the Lord of Creatures</gloss>, referred to as gods and demons based on their functions ... 34

# वैलक्षण्याच्च ।। 2.4.19 ।।

## ।। 2.4.19 ।।

वैलक्षण्यं च भवति, मुख्यस्य इतरेषां च--- सुप्तेषु वागादिषु मुख्य एको जागर्ति; स एव च एको मृत्युना अनाप्तः, आप्तास्त्वितरे, तस्यैव च स्थित्युत्क्रान्तिभ्यां देहधारणपतनहेतुत्वम्, न इन्द्रियाणाम्; विषयालोचनहेतुत्वं च इन्द्रियाणाम्, न प्राणस्य--- इत्येवंजातीयको भूयाँल्लक्षणभेदः प्राणेन्द्रियाणाम्; तस्मादप्येषां तत्त्वान्तरभावसिद्धिः । यदुक्तम्--- ' त एतस्यैव सर्वे रूपमभवन् ' इति श्रुतेः प्राण एवेन्द्रियाणीति, तद्युक्तम्, तत्रापि पौर्वापर्यालोचनाद्भेदप्रतीतेः; तथा हि--- ' वदिष्याम्येवाहमिति वाग्दध्रे ' इति वागादीनीन्द्रियाण्यनुक्रम्य, ' तानि मृत्युः श्रमो भूत्वोपयेमे तस्माच्छ्राम्यत्येव वाक् ' इति च श्रमरूपेण मृत्युना ग्रस्तत्वं वागादीनामभिधाय, ' अथैममेव नाप्नोद्योऽयं मध्यमः प्राणः ' इति पृथक् प्राणं मृत्युना अनभिभूतं तमनुक्रामति; ' अयं वै नः श्रेष्ठः ' इति च श्रेष्ठतामस्यावधारयति, तस्मात् तदविरोधेन, वागादिषु परिस्पन्दलाभस्य प्राणायतत्तवम्--तद्रूपभवनं वागादीनाम्--इति मन्तव्यम्, न तु तादात्म्यम् । अत एव च प्राणशब्दस्येन्द्रियेषु लाक्षणिकत्वसिद्धिः; तथा च श्रुतिः--- ' त एतस्यैव सर्वे रूपमभवन् । तस्मादेत एतेनाख्यायन्ते प्राणाः ' इति मुख्यप्राणविषयस्यैव प्राणशब्दस्येन्द्रियेषु लाक्षणिकों वृत्तिं दर्शयति । तस्मात्तत्त्वान्तराणि प्राणात् वागादीनि इन्द्रियाणीति ।।

# संज्ञामूर्तिक्लृप्तिस्तु त्रिवृत्कुर्वत उपदेशात् ।। 2.4.20 ।।

## संज्ञामूर्तिक्लृप्त्यधिकरणम् ।। 2.4.20 ।।

सत्प्रक्रियायां तेजोबन्नानां सृष्टिमिधायोपदिश्यते--- ' सेयं देवतैक्षत हन्ताहमिमास्तिस्रो देवता अनेन जीवेनात्मनानुप्रविश्य नामरूपे व्याकरवाणीति । तासां त्रिवृतं त्रिवृतमेकैकां करवाणीति ' तत्र संशयः---किं जीवकर्तृकमिदं नामरूपव्याकरणम्, आहोस्वित्परमेश्वरकर्तृकमिति । तत्र प्राप्तं तावत्---जीवकर्तृकमेवेदं नामरूपव्याकरणमिति; कुतः ? ' अनेन जीवेनात्मना ' इति विशेषणात्-- यथा लोके ' चारेणाहं परसैन्यमनुप्रविश्य संकलयानि ' इत्येवंजातीयके प्रयोगे, चारकर्तृकमेव सत् सैन्यसंकलनं हेतुकर्तृत्वात् राजा आत्मन्यध्यारोपयति संकलयानीत्युत्तमपुरुषप्रयोगेण; एवं जीवकर्तृकमेव सत् नामरूपव्याकरणं हेतुकर्तृत्वात् देवता आत्मन्यध्यारोपयति व्याकरवाणीत्युत्तमपुरुषप्रयोगेण । अपि च डित्थडवित्थादिषु नामसु घटशरावादिषु च रूपेषु जीवस्यैव व्याकर्तृत्वं दृष्टम् । तस्माज्जीवकतुकमेवेदं नामरूपव्याकरणमित्येवं प्राप्ते---

अभिधत्ते--- संज्ञामूर्तिक्लृप्तिस्त्विति । तु-शब्देन पक्षं व्यावर्तयति । संज्ञामूर्तिक्लृप्तिरिति-- नामरूपव्याक्रियेत्येतत्; त्रिवृत्कुर्वत इति परमेश्वरं लक्षयति, त्रिवृत्करणे तस्य निरपवादकर्तृत्वनिर्देशात्--येयं संञ्ञाक्लृप्तिः मूर्तिक्लृप्ति च, अग्निः आदित्यः चन्द्रमाः विद्युदिति, तथा कुशकाशपलाशादिषु पशुमृगमनुष्यादिषु च, प्रत्याकृति प्रतिव्यक्ति च अनेकप्रकारा, सा खलु परमेश्वरस्यैव तेजोबन्नानां निर्मातुः कृतिर्भवितुमर्हति; कुतः ? उपदेशात्; तथा हि--- ' सेयं देवता ' इत्युपक्रम्य ' व्याकरवाणि ' इत्युत्तमपुरुषप्रयोगेण परस्यैव ब्रह्मणो व्याकर्तृत्वमिहोपदिश्यते । ननु ' जीवेन ' इति विशेषणात् जीवकर्तृत्वं व्याकरणस्याध्यवसितम्---नैतदेवम्; ' जीवेन ' इत्येतत् ' अनुप्रविश्य ' इत्यनेन संबध्यते, आनन्तर्यात्; न ' व्याकरवाणि ' इत्यनेन-- तेन हि संबन्धे ' व्याकरवाणि ' इत्ययं देवताविषय उत्तमपुरुष औपचारिकः कल्प्येत; न च गिरिनदीसमुद्रादिषु नानाविधेषु नामरूपेषु अनीश्वरस्य जीवस्य व्याकरणसामर्थ्यमस्ति; येष्वपि च अस्ति सामर्थ्यम्, तेष्वपि परमेश्वरायत्तमेव तत्; न च जीवो नाम परमेश्वरादत्यन्तभिन्नः-- चार इव राज्ञः, ' आत्मना ' इति विशेषणात्, उपाधिमात्रनिबन्धनत्वाच्च जीवभावस्य; तेन तत्कृतमपि नामरूपव्याकरणं परमेश्वरकृतमेव

<meta>Continuity: The previous page established that the individual soul (Jiva) is the master of the vital breaths and the senses, rather than the presiding deities. This page begins by proving that the Chief Vital Breath (Mukhya Prāṇa) is a distinct entity from the other sensory organs (Indriyas) and moves into a new section regarding who is responsible for the creation of names and forms in the universe.</meta>

"He made speech and the breath for himself" <note>original: "vācaṃ prāṇaṃ tānyātmane'kuruta" from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3</note>. Scriptural passages such as this, which show the distinction between the breath and the senses, should also be cited here. Therefore, it is settled that the others (the senses) are distinct principles from the Chief Breath.

Why else are they considered distinct principles?

# Because of their Distinct Characteristics (2.4.19)
## 2.4.19

There is indeed a distinction <term>vailakṣaṇya; a difference in essential nature or characteristics</term> between the Chief Breath and the others (the sense organs). When the organs of speech and the rest are asleep, the Chief Breath alone remains awake. He alone is untouched by death, while the others are overtaken by it. Furthermore, it is the stay or departure of the Chief Breath that causes the body to be sustained or to fall, not the senses. The senses are the cause of perceiving objects, but the breath is not. In this way, there are many differences in characteristics between the Breath and the senses; for this reason also, the fact that they are distinct principles is established.

As for the argument that "All these became a form of this [the Breath]" <note>original: "ta etasyaiva sarve rūpamabhavan" from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21</note> implies that the senses are nothing but the Breath, that is incorrect. Even in that context, a distinction is understood by looking at the preceding and following passages. For instance, the scripture begins by listing the senses—speech and the rest—saying, "Speech held the vow: 'I will surely speak.'" It then describes how they were overtaken by death in the form of weariness: "Death, taking the form of weariness, overtook them; therefore, speech grows weary." After this, it separately lists the Breath as being unvanquished by death: "But death did not reach this one, which is the middle breath." It further determines its superiority by saying, "This one is indeed the best among us." Therefore, to avoid contradicting these statements, the phrase "they became its form" must be understood to mean that the senses depend on the Breath for their activity, not that they are identical to it. 

Furthermore, this establishes that the word "Breath" <term>prāṇa; used here to denote both the life-force and, metaphorically, the senses</term> is used figuratively when applied to the senses. Thus, the scripture says: "All these became a form of this; therefore, they are called by its name, 'the breaths'" <note>original: "tasmādetat etenākhyāyante prāṇāḥ"</note>. This shows that the word "breath," which primarily refers to the Chief Breath, is used in a secondary or metaphorical sense for the sense organs. Therefore, the organs like speech are principles distinct from the Breath.

# The formation of Names and Forms belongs to Him who renders them Tripartite, because of the Teaching (2.4.20)
## Section on the Formation of Names and Forms (2.4.20)

In the process of creation <term>sat-prakriyā; the Vedantic teaching on the origin of "Being"</term>, after the creation of fire, water, and earth is described, it is taught: "That deity thought: 'Indeed, let me enter these three deities with this living soul and differentiate names and forms. Let me make each of them threefold <term>trivṛtkaraṇa; the process of mixing the three subtle elements to create the gross world</term>.'" 

A doubt arises here: Is this differentiation of names and forms the work of the individual soul <term>jīva</term>, or is it the work of the Supreme Lord <term>parameśvara</term>? 

The initial view suggests that this differentiation of names and forms is the work of the individual soul. Why? Because of the qualification "with this living soul." For example, in common language, when a king says, "I will enter the enemy army with a spy and assess them," the actual assessment is done by the spy, but the king—as the primary cause—attributes the action to himself by using the first person ("I will assess"). In the same way, while the differentiation of names and forms is done by the individual soul, the Deity (the Lord) attributes the action to Himself, saying "I will differentiate" because He is the ultimate cause. Furthermore, in the world, we see that the creation of names like 'Dittha' or 'Davittha,' and forms like pots and jars, is the work of the individual soul. Therefore, it is concluded that the individual soul is the creator of names and forms.

To this, we reply: **The formation of names and forms belongs to Him (the Lord).** The word "but" <term>tu</term> in the sutra refutes the previous view. "Formation of names and forms" <term>saṃjñā-mūrti-klṛpti</term> means the differentiation of names and shapes. The phrase "Him who renders them tripartite" refers to the Supreme Lord, for the scripture attributes the act of making the elements threefold exclusively to Him. 

This formation of names and forms—such as the Sun, the Moon, and lightning, or the various species like grass, trees, cattle, wild animals, and humans, across every genus and individual—must surely be the work of the Supreme Lord, the creator of fire, water, and earth. Why? Because of the teaching. The text begins with "That Deity" and then teaches that the Supreme Brahman is the creator by using the first-person verb "I will differentiate." 

If you argue that the qualification "with the living soul" indicates that the soul is the creator, that is not so. "With the living soul" is connected to the word "entering," because of their proximity in the sentence, not with "I will differentiate." If it were connected to the latter, then the first-person "I will differentiate" would have to be interpreted figuratively as referring to the Deity. Moreover, an individual soul, who is not the Lord, does not have the power to create the vast variety of names and forms found in mountains, rivers, and oceans. Even where the soul does have power (like making pots), that power is entirely dependent on the Supreme Lord. Furthermore, the soul is not absolutely different from the Lord—like a spy is from a king—as shown by the word "self" <term>ātmanā</term> and because the state of being an individual soul is based only on limiting conditions <term>upādhi</term>. Therefore, even that which is done by the soul is ultimately the work of the Supreme Lord.

<summary>This page distinguishes the Chief Vital Breath from the senses and establishes that the Supreme Lord, not the individual soul, is the ultimate creator of the diversity of names and forms in the universe.</summary>

# प्राणवता शब्दात् ।। 2.4.15 ।।
<note>2.4.15</note>

सतीष्वपि प्राणानामधिष्ठात्रीषु देवतासु प्राणवता कार्यकारणसंघातस्वामिना शारीरेणैव एषां प्राणानां संबन्धः श्रुतेरवगम्यते; तथा हि श्रुतिः---` अथ यत्रैतदाकाशमनुविषण्णं चक्षुः स चाक्षुषः पुरुषो दर्शनाय चक्षुरथ यो वेदेदं जिघ्राणीति स आत्मा गन्धाय घ्राणम् ' इत्येवंजातीयका शारीरेण प्राणानां संबन्धं श्रावयति । अपि च अनेकत्वात्प्रतिकरणमधिष्ठात्रीणां देवतानां न भोक्तृत्वम् अस्मिन् शरीरेऽवकल्पते; एको ह्ययमिस्मिन् शरीरे शारीरो भोक्ता प्रतिसंधानादिसंवादवगम्यते ।।

# तस्य च नित्यत्वात् ।। 2.4.16 ।।
<note>2.4.16</note>

तस्य च शारीरस्यास्मिन् शरीरे भोक्तृत्वेन नित्यत्वम्--पुण्यपापोपलेपसंभवात् सुखदुःखोपभोगसंभवाच्च, न देवतानाम्; ता हि परस्मिन्नैश्वर्ये पदेऽवतिष्ठमाना न हीनेऽस्मिन् शरीरे भोक्तृत्वं प्रतिलब्धुमर्हन्ति; श्रुति च भवति--- ` पुण्यमेवामुं गच्छति न ह वै देवान्पापं गच्छति ' इति । शारीरेणैव च नित्यः प्राणानां संबन्धः, उत्क्रान्त्यादिषु तदनुवृत्तिदर्शनात्-- - ` तमुत्क्रामन्तं प्राणोऽनूत्क्रामति प्राणमनूत्क्रामन्तं सर्वे प्राणा अनूत्क्रामन्ति ' इत्यादिश्रुतिभ्यः । तस्मात् सतीष्वपि करणानां नियन्त्रीषु देवतासु न शारीरस्य भोक्तृत्वमपगच्छति; करणपक्षस्यैव हि देवता, न भोक्तृपक्षस्येति ।।

# त इन्द्रियाणि तद्व्यपदेशादन्यत्र श्रेष्ठात् ।। 2.4.17 ।।
->इन्द्रियाधिकरणम् ।। 2.4.17 ।।<-
<note>2.4.17</note>

मुख्यश्चैकः इतरे चैकादश प्राणा अनुक्रान्ताः; तत्रेदं परं संदिह्यते--- किं मुख्यस्यैव प्राणस्य वृत्तिभेदा इतरे प्राणाः, आहोस्वित् तत्त्वान्तराणीति । किं तावत्प्राप्तम्---मुख्यस्यैवेतारे वृत्तिभेदा इति; कुतः ? श्रुतेः; तथा हि श्रुतिः मुख्यमितरां च प्राणान्संनिधाप्य, मुख्यताममितेरेषां ख्यापयति--- ` हन्तास्यैव सर्वे रूपमसामेति त एतस्यैव सर्वे रूपमभवन् ' इति; प्राणैकशब्दाच्चैकत्वमध्यवसायः; इतरथा ह्यन्याय्यमनेकार्थत्वं प्राणशब्दस्य प्रसज्येत, एकत्र वा मुख्यस्येतरत्र लाक्षणिकत्वमापद्येत । तस्माद्यथैकस्यैव प्राणस्य प्राणाद्याः पञ्च वृत्तयः, एवं वागाद्या अप्येकादशेति; एवं प्राप्ते, ब्रूमः--- तत्त्वान्तराण्येव प्राणाद्वागादीनीति; कुतः ? व्यपदेशभेदात्; कोऽयं व्यपदेशभेदः ? ते प्रकृताः प्राणाः, श्रेष्ठं वर्जयित्वा अवशिष्टा एकादशेन्द्रियाणीत्युच्यन्ते, श्रुतावेवं व्यपदेशभेददर्शनात्--- ` एतस्माज्जायते प्राणो मनः सर्वेन्द्रियाणि च इति ह्येवंजातीयकेषु प्रदेशेषु पृथक् प्राणो व्यपदिश्यते, पृथक्च इन्द्रियाणि । ननु मनसोऽप्येवं सति वर्जनम् इन्द्रियत्वेन, प्राणवत्, स्यात्-- ` मनः सर्वेन्द्रियाणि च ' इति पृथग्व्यपदेशदर्शनात्; सत्यमेतत्--- स्मृतौ तु एकादशेन्द्रियाणीति मनोऽपि इन्द्रियत्वेन श्रोत्रादिवत् संगृह्यते; प्राणस्य तु इन्द्रियत्वं न श्रुतौ स्मृतौ वा प्रसिद्धमस्ति । व्यपदेशभेद चायं तत्त्वभेदपक्षे उपपद्यते; तत्त्वैकत्वे तु, स एवैकः सन् प्राण इन्द्रियव्यपदेशं लभते न लभते च-- इति विप्रतिषिद्धम् । तस्मात्तत्त्वान्तरभूता मुख्यादितरे ।।

कुत च तत्त्वान्तरभूताः ?---

# भेदश्रुतेः ।। 2.4.18 ।।
<note>2.4.18</note>

<meta>Continuity: The previous page concluded the discussion on the five-fold functions of the Vital Breath (Prāṇa), comparing them to the functions of the mind. This page begins by establishing that the individual soul, rather than the presiding deities, is the true master of these life-functions and explores the distinction between the Chief Breath and the sensory organs.</meta>

# The Connection is with the Possessor of Breath, according to Scripture (2.4.15)
<note>2.4.15</note>

Even though there are presiding deities <term>devatā; celestial beings who govern natural and bodily functions</term> over the vital breaths, it is understood from the scriptures that these breaths are connected to the embodied soul <term>śārīra; the individual self dwelling in the body</term>, who is the master of the aggregate of the body and its causes and effects. For the scripture declares: "Now, where the eye is directed toward space, that is the person in the eye for the sake of seeing; and he who knows 'I smell this,' he is the Self, and the nose is for smelling" <note>original: "atha yatraita-ākāśam-anuviṣaṇṇaṃ cakṣuḥ..." from the Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.4</note>. This and similar passages declare the connection of the vital breaths with the embodied soul. Furthermore, because there are many presiding deities, one for each organ, it is not possible for them to be the "experiencer" <term>bhoktṛ; the one who feels pleasure and pain</term> in this body. In this body, there is only one embodied soul who is understood to be the experiencer, based on the fact that one person coordinates all their different perceptions.

# And because of its Permanence (2.4.16)
<note>2.4.16</note>

Moreover, the embodied soul’s status as the experiencer in this body is permanent—because of the possibility of being affected by merit and demerit <term>puṇya and pāpa; good and bad karma</term> and the possibility of experiencing pleasure and pain. This is not true for the deities. They, who remain in a state of supreme lordship, are not fit to be experiencers in this lowly body. And the scripture says: "Only merit goes to him; no evil, indeed, goes to the gods" <note>original: "puṇyamevāmuṃ gacchati..." from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.20</note>. Also, the connection of the vital breaths with the embodied soul is permanent, as we see them following the soul during its departure and other states. As the scriptures say: "When he departs, the Life-Breath departs after him; and when the Life-Breath departs, all the other breaths depart after it" <note>original: "tam-utkrāmantaṃ prāṇo'nūtkrāmati..." from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2</note>. Therefore, even though the deities are the controllers of the organs, the embodied soul does not lose its status as the experiencer; for the deities belong to the "side of the instruments" (the organs), not the "side of the experiencer."

# They are the Senses, because of their separate designation, except for the Chief (2.4.17)
->Section on the Senses (2.4.17)<-
<note>2.4.17</note>

The Chief Breath <note>original: "mukhya-prāṇa"</note> is one, and the other eleven breaths have been enumerated. Now, a doubt arises: Are the other breaths merely different functions of the Chief Breath, or are they distinct realities? What is the initial view? That the others are merely variations of the Chief Breath. Why? Because of the scripture. For the scripture, placing the Chief Breath and the other breaths together, shows the others to be forms of the Chief: "Well, let us all take his form; and they all became his form" <note>original: "hantāsyaiva sarve rūpamasāmeti..." from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21</note>. Also, since the word "Breath" <note>original: "prāṇa"</note> is used for all of them, we conclude they are one; otherwise, it would be improper to give multiple meanings to the same word "Breath," or we would have to assume the word is used literally in one case and figuratively in the others. Therefore, just as the five-fold breaths like Prāṇa and the rest are functions of one Breath, so too are the eleven organs like speech.

To this, we reply: The organs like speech are distinct realities from the Chief Breath. Why? Because of the difference in designation. What is this difference? Those breaths under discussion, excluding the Chief, are called the eleven "senses" <term>indriya; the faculties of perception and action</term>, for such a difference in designation is seen in the scripture: "From Him are born the Breath, the mind, and all the organs/senses" <note>original: "etasmāj-jāyate prāṇo manaḥ sarvendriyāṇi ca" from the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.3</note>. In such passages, the Breath is designated separately, and the senses are designated separately. 

One might object: "In that case, the mind should also be excluded from being a sense-organ, just like the Breath, because it is mentioned separately in the phrase 'the mind and all the senses'." This is true; however, in the Smriti <term>traditional texts like the Bhagavad Gita or Manu Smriti</term>, the mind is included as a sense-organ along with the ear and others in the count of eleven. But the Chief Breath is never famously known as a "sense" <note>original: "indriya"</note> in either the primary scriptures (Shruti) or traditional law (Smriti). This difference in designation makes sense only if there is a difference in reality. If they were the same reality, it would be contradictory for the same Breath to be called a "sense" and not be called a "sense" at the same time. Therefore, the others are distinct realities from the Chief.

And why else are they distinct realities?

# Because of the scriptural mention of difference (2.4.18)
<note>2.4.18</note>

Everywhere in the scriptures, the Breath is mentioned as different from speech and the others. Starting with "They spoke to Speech," the text describes how speech and the others were struck by the evil of the demons; then, having concluded the section on speech and the rest, it begins a separate section for the Chief Breath, which destroyed the demons: "Then they spoke to this Breath in the mouth" <note>original: "atha hemam-āsanyaṃ prāṇam-ūcuḥ" from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.2-7</note>. *Acceditur ad spiritus ministros, bonos malosque: quorum utrosque negarunt Saducæi; item Democritus; ex parte etiam Aristoteles: at contrà eos agnoverunt Pythagorici, & Platonici: atque ut doctrina hæc ad gentiles etiam à majoribus, multorum seculorum traditione, sit derivata: quadruplici item ratione comprobata, spectris, oraculis, magicis artibus, & prodigiis. Angelis sui generis corpus tribui, non modo à philosophis, sed etiam multis Sanctorum Patrum. In quo gentiles, & alii, de natura eorum aberrarint.*

Dictum de duplici spiritu, uno boni, altero mali principio; quorum utrumque pari, vel suppari honore coluerint. Eâque occasione etiam vidimus de variis opinionibus, quæ inde promanarint; sed dissimili ratione; dum alii non duo statuunt principia, sed multa; sic tamen divisa, ut quædam essent benefica, quædam malefica; ac utrisque cultus præstaretur divinus: alii autem, ut Manichæi, duo duntaxat principia, boni unum, alterum mali, constituerent; soli tamen principio boni cultum, ut Deo, exhiberent. Deinceps accedo ad spiritus, non principes, sed ministros: qui à philosophis communi nomine fere dæmones vel dæmonia, à Peripateticis intelligentiæ, à Christianis boni malive angeli appellantur.

In his considerabimus, naturam, officium, & cultum. In natura spectabimus hæc tria: primum, qui spiritus hosce negarint, qui agnorint: deinde unde eos gentes cognoverint: & quatenus in eorum natura convenerint Christiani, ac gentiles: denique de naturæ hujus præstantia; quæ ex cultus caussis una fuit.

Spiritus non agnovere Saducæi: ut est Actorum xxiii, 8. Objectant nobis Iudæi, quòd libros Mosaicos agnoscerent pro divinis; ubi sæpius commemoratur, ut angeli apparuerint. Verùm verisimile mihi fit, Saducæos eludere hæc solitos: cujus ratio nunc gemina occurrit. Vna est, ut per eas non aliud intellexerint, quàm qualitates à Deo productas in imaginatione ejus, quem de re aliqua velit edocere. ### CHAPTER VI.

*We proceed to the ministering spirits, both good and bad. Both were denied by the Sadducees, as well as by Democritus, and in part even by Aristotle. On the contrary, the Pythagoreans and Platonists acknowledged them. This doctrine was derived even by the gentiles from their ancestors through a tradition of many centuries. It is proven by a fourfold reason: ghosts, oracles, magical arts, and portents. A body of its own kind is attributed to angels, not only by philosophers but also by many of the Holy Fathers. We will consider in what way the gentiles and others have erred regarding their nature.*

We have spoken about the twofold spirit, one the principle of good and the other of evil, both of which were worshipped with equal or nearly equal honor. On that occasion, we also saw the various opinions that flowed from this idea, though in different ways. Some do not establish only two principles but many. These were divided so that some were beneficial and some harmful, and divine worship was offered to both. Others, however, like the Manichaeans <note>A dualistic religious movement that saw the world as a struggle between light and darkness.</note>, established only two principles, one of good and the other of evil, yet they offered worship only to the principle of good as if to God. Next, I proceed to the spirits who are not rulers but ministers. These are commonly called demons or spirits <note>original: "dæmones vel dæmonia"</note> by the philosophers, intelligences by the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</note>, and good or evil angels by Christians.

In these beings, we will consider their nature, their office, and their worship. Regarding their nature, we will look at these three things: first, who denied these spirits and who acknowledged them; next, from where the nations <note>Specifically the non-Jewish or "gentile" nations of antiquity.</note> learned of them; and to what extent Christians and gentiles agreed on their nature. Finally, we will consider the excellence of this nature, which was one of the reasons for their worship.

The Sadducees did not acknowledge spirits, as is written in Acts 23:8. The Jews object to us that the Sadducees accepted the Mosaic books as divine, where it is frequently mentioned that angels appeared. However, it seems likely to me that the Sadducees were accustomed to evade these passages. Two reasons for this now occur to me. One is that they understood these appearances as nothing other than qualities produced by God in the imagination of the person he wished to teach about some matter. The other is that they thought God produces spirits only when he wishes to use their labor and destroys them afterward. They thought he produced them by separating something from the world soul <term>anima mundana</term> <note>a vital force or spirit believed by some ancient philosophers to animate the entire universe</note>, which would later return to the general nature.

Among the philosophers of the nations, Democritus did not acknowledge any spirits. Nor did Aristotle, except for the movers of the celestial spheres. Dixeris, ut hoc ita ſit in quibuſdam; tamen eſſe ex venenis innumera, ex quibus nullam homines, vel muta animantia capiant utilitatem: atque hoc facilè appariturum circumferenti animum per ea, quæ de his legere eſt, vel apud Græcos, ut Nicandrum, Dioſcoridem, Aëtium, Æginetam; vel Arabas, ut Avicennam, Serapionem, Hali abbatem, Rhaſin; vel recentiores Latinos, ut Petrum Aponenſem, Sanctem de Arduinis, cardinalem Ponzettum; ut Cardanum, Grevinum, Mercurialem, alioſque prætereamus. Sed enim ſcimus & multorum ex illis utilitatem inſignem prodi ab iis, qui in arcanis naturæ rimandis ſtudium & operam collocarunt: & ſi de omnibus id oſtendere non poſſumus, non eo malignitatis culpanda eſt natura, vel ejus auctor; ſed inertiæ id noſtræ tribuendum, qui non, quantum poteramus, curæ & diligentiæ in indagando eorum uſu poſuerimus. Quid quod ſic quoque ex venenis illis utilitas ad nos redit? Excitant enim induſtriam noſtram in diſcernendis ſalubribus à venenatis. Patientiæ quoque materiem hinc habemus. <meta>This page continues the argument against the Manichaean worldview. It addresses the existence of natural "evils" like poison. Vossius argues that these substances are not evidence of an evil creator, but are either misunderstood benefits or reminders of human fallenness.</meta>

# BOOK I ON IDOLATRY

...those who have considered these things more studiously. For if the poet from Sulmo <note>Ovid, who was born in Sulmo, Italy.</note> said in the second book of his *Tristia*:
> Nothing is useful that cannot also cause harm. <note>Original Latin: *Nil prodest, quod non lædere possit idem.*</note>

I might say with no less justice:
> Nothing harms that does not also bring certain benefits. <note>Original Latin: *Nil lædit, quod non commoda certa ferat.*</note>

Therefore, if something causes harm, it should not immediately be considered a thing that inconveniences the nature of things. For what is harmful in one place is helpful in another. Who is ignorant of how much danger hemlock <note>A highly poisonous herbaceous flowering plant.</note> puts men into? I have an illustrious example of this matter involving my own relatives. It was mentioned by the noble Henricus Smetius <note>A 16th-century physician and scholar.</note>, a man very closely linked to me by marriage while he lived, in the tenth book of his *Medical Miscellanies*, in the observations for the year <term>1591</term>. Yet, among the Taurini of Liguria <note>An ancient Celtic-Ligurian people in the area of modern-day Turin, Italy.</note>, it is considered food that is not only delicate but also healthy, and suitable for promoting urine among other things. How many poisons to man exist in foods that benefit him in medicines! And even if they were of no use or benefit for either reason, they would still bring advantage to man by serving as food for mute animals, which later yield to us as nourishment or medicine. Lucretius expressed this skillfully in these verses in his fourth book:
> And so great is the distance and difference in these things,
> That what is food to some, is sharp poison to others.
> Thus there is a serpent which, touched by human saliva,
> Perishes, and consumes itself by gnawing.
> Furthermore, hellebore <term>veratrum</term> <note>A genus of poisonous herbs often used in ancient medicine.</note> is a sharp poison to us,
> But it increases the fat in goats and quails.

You might say that while this may be so in certain cases, there are nonetheless innumerable poisons from which neither men nor mute animals derive any utility. This would easily appear to anyone who turns his mind through those things one can read about them. This is true whether looking at the Greeks, such as Nicander, Dioscorides, Aetius, or Aegineta; or the Arabs, such as Avicenna, Serapion, Hali Abbas, and Rhazes; or more recent Latin authors, such as Peter of Abano, Santes de Ardoynis, and Cardinal Ponzetti; not to mention Cardano, Grevin, Mercuriale, and others. <note>Vossius lists a massive directory of medical and toxicological authorities from antiquity through the Renaissance to show the depth of human study on the subject.</note> But indeed, we know that a remarkable utility for many of those substances is put forward by those who have placed their study and labor into searching the secrets of nature. Even if we cannot show this for all of them, nature or its author <note>God.</note> is not to be blamed for malice. Instead, it must be attributed to our own laziness, because we have not applied as much care and diligence as we could in investigating their use. What of the fact that utility returns to us from those poisons in this way too? They excite our industry in discerning healthy things from poisonous ones. We also have material for patience from this. When we see how many dangers this life is subject to, we recognize more clearly the wrath of God toward sin, because of which...

<meta>The catchword at the bottom of the page is "quod" (which).</meta>

<summary>Vossius argues that poisons and natural harms are not inherently evil but serve hidden purposes in nature, medicine, or as divine reminders of human mortality and sin.</summary>
<keywords>toxicology, Lucretius, Ovid, natural philosophy, medicine, hemlock, providence, theodicy, sin</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the alchemical instructions attributed to Rosinus (the Latinized name for Zosimos of Panopolis), specifically from the "Letter to Sarratant." It clarifies the nature of the "Stone" by explaining that while it is said to be "within" the alchemist, this is a metaphor for knowledge and elemental composition rather than a literal physical byproduct of the human body.</meta>

# TO SARRATANT

<page-num>311</page-num>

...but because they are similar, they are mixed together and joined, so much so that fire does not separate us <note>original: "non ſeparet inter nos"; likely meaning the elements within the compound or the bond between the alchemist's spirit and the work</note>. Therefore, take the **Stone of Rebis** <term>Rebis</term> <note>original: "lapidem Rebis"; from the Latin "res bina," meaning "double-thing." It represents the union of opposites, such as male and female or spirit and matter, into a single substance</note>: that is, two things, namely the moist and the cold, [and] the dry and the hot. Whence **Rhazes** <note>original: "Raſis"; Abu Bakr al-Razi, a 9th-century Persian alchemist and physician</note> and **Morienus** <note>A legendary hermit-alchemist said to have taught the secrets of the Stone to King Khalid ibn Yazid</note> say: What secret then will you expect in vanishing humors, from which it begets children? Our stone is hot and dry. Whence the verse: *Mountains give dragons to things, and springs in the earth.* Therefore, take this **animal stone** <note>original: "lapidem animalem"; in alchemy, "animal" refers to the "anima" or soul/life-force within a substance, not necessarily a creature</note>: that is, having a soul within itself, namely the **sensible Mercurial** <note>original: "Mercurialem ſenſibile"; mercury that is active and responsive to influence</note>: that is, sensing the presence and influence of **magnesia** <note>original: "magneſiæ"; a term used in alchemy for various transformative mineral ores</note>, and of the **magnet** <note>original: "magnetis"</note>, and of **calamine** <note>original: "calaminaré"; a zinc ore</note>, and the summit through local motion, pursuing and putting to flight the **vegetable** <note>original: "vegetabilem"; here referring to the power of growth or the "spirit" of the substance</note>: that is, its power implanted in nature, communicating to its own kind, multiplying the power of its influence, like a root to a trunk, a mineral without herbs: because it is extracted from a mine.

Whence certain people, poorly understanding the Philosophers, say: "This stone is such a thing that is fixed more in you, created by God, and you are its mine, and it is extracted from you, and wherever you are, it remains with you inseparably." They thought from this that it was human hair, blood, or dung; but they are fools when they say "it is fixed in him": that is, there [within yourself] you have its knowledge, and not in any other thing. And just as man is composed of the **four elements** <note>original: "4. elementis"; earth, air, fire, and water</note>, so also is the stone; and so it is "from man," and you are its "mine"—namely, through the **Great Work** <term>operation</term> <note>original: "operationem"</note>—and it is "extracted from you"—namely, through division—and "remains in you inseparably"—namely, through knowledge.

<meta>This page continues the compilation of alchemical authorities (Rosinus/Zosimos) defining the nature of the Philosopher's Stone. It moves from the biological metaphors of the previous page into the specific chemical and elemental requirements for the Work, citing figures such as Geber, Aristotle, and the elusive "Mitigo."</meta>

# ROSINUS

<page-num>310</page-num>

...no division occurs in it, nor any conflict, and you will have your goal, God granting it. **Mitigo the Philosopher** <note>Likely a Latinized corruption of an Arabic authority, possibly Masarjawaih or a similar figure cited in medieval alchemical compendiums</note> says: Our Stone, although it is trodden underfoot by men and animals, nonetheless, because of the diligence of the man **Geber** <note>Abu Musa Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the most famous figure in Islamic alchemy, known for emphasizing systematic experimentation</note>, it is loved by the wise. And he mentions "diligence": because it is produced by the diligence of the man Geber. Likewise, **Malus the Philosopher** <note>Perhaps a corruption of a name like Magnes or Morienus; the name "Malus" literally means "the Evil One" in Latin, but here likely serves as a shorthand for a specific teacher</note> says: This stone is beneath you, regarding obedience; above you, regarding dominion; therefore from you, regarding knowledge; and around you, regarding its equals.

**Aristotle** <note>Referring to "Pseudo-Aristotle," the author of various medieval alchemical texts attributed to the Greek philosopher</note>: I shall name our stone; it is the boundary of the soul <note>original: "terminus ani"; likely a corruption of "animae" (soul)</note>. For it is the **Philosophers' Egg** <term>Philosophers' Egg</term> <note>original: "ouum Philoſophorum"; a central metaphor for the sealed vessel containing the "yolk" and "white" (sulfur and mercury) which hatches into the Stone</note> which exists in putrefaction and purification. Divide it, therefore, into the four elements. This division occurs in two ways: that is, without the corruption of the **Sun** and **Moon** <note>original: "Solis & Lunae"; alchemical code for Gold and Silver</note>. This division is universal in terms of the understanding, but the second division divides it into specific operations. When, therefore, you have obtained water from air, and air from fire, and fire from earth, and each of these divided by itself, you will fully possess the art.

Take, therefore, from the stone found everywhere, which is called **Rebis** <term>Rebis</term> <note>original: "res bina," meaning "the double thing"; it represents the hermaphroditic or dual nature of the primary material before it is unified</note>, and it is born in two mountains, from which flying spirits take in vain; and you shall not receive it unless it is fresh with its own blood, whose food is from blood, and it dwells in the air. And if this stone were not airy, or of an airy nature, it would not be joined to **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurio"</note>, nor would it be mixed with it, nor would it enter into it:

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Giovanni Aurelio Augurello’s alchemical poetry. It moves from the theoretical existence of "seeds" in metals to a specific poetic description of how a craftsman can release the life force within gold. It then provides a real-world example of "growing gold" in the vineyards of Hungary to prove that minerals possess a form of life.</meta>

## Of Occult Philosophy

<margin>
The species of the female principle are to be restrained; if these are rightly preserved according to nature... Wherefore Augurellus in his book... for gold... it is necessary for the latent spirit to be released from the blind darkness into the open air. In gold, the seed of this thing is found through labor, rather than from other spirits.
</margin>

> Finally, even when detained in yellow gold,
> The spirit itself desires the hand of the craftsman to loosen its chains,
> And to restore its power through its own inherent virtue.
> If any craftsman, working with haste, should ever
> Unfold this by the powers of the art, and cook it long over a warm fire,
> You will immediately behold a wonder: life
> Is bestowed upon the gold through the long application of the seed.

One must also observe which stars <note>in this context, the word refers to the five visible planets, the Sun, and the Moon</note> primarily transit the general places. These movements are very important for identifying when events will happen. In the general places, the principal power belongs to Saturn and Jupiter in the yearly periods. <meta>This page concludes the introductory argument about the causes of aging and the role of the humors, specifically phlegm, before transitioning into Chapter III. It continues the previous page's discussion on how physicians must protect the life force from two opposing threats: "dissolution" (drying out) and "suffocation" (drowning in excess fluids).</meta>

...happens by a certain internal faction: especially when phlegm <note>original: *pituita* — one of the four humors, associated with cold and moisture</note> either overflows or becomes putrefied in some way; thus it was not without reason that phlegm was named "the seeker of life" <note>original: *pituita petes vitam* — a wordplay suggesting that excess phlegm "seeks" or attacks the life force</note>. Therefore, these are the precepts most necessary for prolonging life. On the one hand, they avoid dissolution <note>original: *resolutio* — the leaking away or evaporation of the body's vital heat and moisture</note>; on the other, they equally avoid suffocation <note>original: *suffocatio* — the extinguishing of the vital spark by an excess of cold, damp fluids</note> and putrefaction.

They do so, I say, by a common principle. For if they happen to treat a man who is naturally warmer or drier, and whose channels <note>original: *meatus* — the pores and pathways in the body</note> are open, then the humors and the subtle spirits <note>original: *spiritus* — the refined "air" that carries life through the nerves and arteries</note> are more prone to dissolution. But if they treat a body affected by the opposite condition, they instead come to the aid of suffocation. They strive especially toward one or the other if the location or the time of year leans in that direction. 

But when providing counsel for the ingenious and the studious <note>scholars, writers, and intellectuals who were Ficino’s primary audience</note>, both precepts are almost equally necessary, and one must labor similarly in both directions. For in these people, a sharp and hot intellect and the constant movement of the imagination threaten dissolution; yet the leisure of the body and indigestion <note>original: *cruditas* — literally "rawness," referring to undigested food that creates blockages</note> seem to threaten suffocation. Nowhere, therefore, do physicians labor more intensely than in the care of such men. And although the entire discussion of the previous book contributes greatly to prolonging life, such a great matter seems to demand its own specific care, which I shall hereafter summarize in a few words as best I can.

### How Heat Must Be Balanced with Moisture, and Vice Versa, by a Certain Counsel of Minerva. Chapter III.

Furthermore, while we treat this rich oil—so necessary for our fiery vigor—with "plain common sense" <note>original: *pingui Minerva* — a Latin idiom meaning "with a thick Minerva," or simple, unrefined wisdom</note>, Minerva herself, the olive-bearer and origin of the vital oil, born from the head of nourishing Jove, smiles. She smiles because while we clearly saw the quantity of her gift, we did not meanwhile sufficiently see its quality. Laughing, therefore, she says: "I have given you oil in abundance, not only enough to nourish the flame, but also pure oil, without the dregs <note>original: *amurca* — the watery, bitter sediment of olive oil</note>, to be poured into the lamp."

Thus she spoke. But we, wandering as we spoke, stumbled; because the lamp was "a word to our feet" <note>A play on Psalm 119:105, "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet"</note>, though its meaning was not yet heard by us. From this lamp, therefore, let us learn that oil must be constantly supplied to the flame with such diligence that we do not overwhelm the light with a sudden flooding. Nor, on the other hand, should we delay giving drink to the thirsty flame. But these two matters we think have been sufficiently treated in the preceding sections. Two things remain for us: one of which I have touched upon lightly, and the other...

<summary>Ficino explains that scholars face a double danger: their intense mental activity dries them out (dissolution), while their sedentary lifestyle leads to a buildup of harmful fluids (suffocation). He introduces a metaphor using Minerva and her olive oil to explain the balance of "fuel" needed for the body's vital lamp.</summary>

<keywords>phlegm, dissolution, suffocation, scholars' health, humors, vital spirit, Minerva, olive oil, balance of heat and moisture</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the first chapter of Ficino’s "On Long Life," moving from the necessity of knowledge to the physiological requirements for a long lifespan. It transitions from the idea that while fate sets a beginning, human diligence can extend the end.</meta>

...to achieve through habit. Indeed, the Fates do not only permit a long life once and for all from the beginning: but our own diligence also provides it. This is something both astrologers admit—when they discuss "elections" <note>original: "electionibus" — the astrological practice of choosing the most auspicious time to begin an undertaking</note> and the use of images—and which the diligent care and experience of physicians confirms. Through such prudence, not only are naturally strong men very often preserved, but even the sickly <note>original: "valitudinarii" — those with delicate or chronic health conditions</note> sometimes achieve a long life. Thus, it is no wonder that a certain **Herodicus** <note>A 5th-century BC Greek physician and teacher of Hippocrates known for using exercise to treat his own frail health</note>, a lover of letters and the most infirm man of his time (as **Plato** and **Aristotle** testify), reached his hundredth year through such prudence. **Plutarch** moreover relates that many who otherwise had a poorly firm body achieved a long life through diligence alone. I will omit for now how many weak people I myself have known who, by the gift of prudence, have surpassed the years of the most robust. 

Therefore, it will be neither useless nor in vain—following the book we composed on caring for the health of scholars—to hand down certain additional precepts for minds thirsty for knowledge that lead to a long life. However, we do not wish these instructions to be shared with the idle and the lazy. For why should we desire for those people to live long? They do not truly live at all; it would be as if we were nourishing drones rather than bees. Nor should they be spread among men lost to the lust for pleasures, who foolishly prefer a brief daily pleasure to a long life. Nor should they be revealed to the wicked and the unjust, whose life is the death of the good. Rather, these are for prudent and temperate men alone, whose skillful mental powers will benefit the human race either privately or publicly.

### Vital heat is nourished by moisture: When it is lacking, dissolution occurs; when it exceeds, suffocation occurs. Chapter 2.

Life, indeed, consists in natural heat, just like a light <note>Ficino uses the metaphor of a lamp flame to represent the "vital heat" of the body.</note>. The fuel for this heat is an airy and fatty moisture, much like oil. If, therefore, such moisture happens to fail, or if it entirely exceeds or becomes tainted, the heat is immediately weakened, and at last, having been weakened, it is extinguished. If the heat is weakened and perishes through a deficiency of moisture, death occurs by **resolution** <note>original: "resolutione" — a process of drying out or "thinning" where the body's substance dissolves away.</note>. If it is instead overwhelmed by an excess or vice of the moisture, life perishes by **suffocation**. This suffocation of any moisture [comes from] its oozing out or putrefaction...

<summary>Ficino argues that diligence and medical prudence can extend life even for the infirm, citing historical figures like Herodicus. He introduces the physiological theory that life is a "vital heat" fueled by bodily moisture, which must be carefully balanced to avoid death by drying out or being overwhelmed by fluids.</summary>

<keywords>vital heat, radical moisture, Herodicus, longevity, medical prudence, Plato, Aristotle, resolution and suffocation, humoral theory</keywords>

> „Ich stehe auf einem Berge, rechts möchte ich hinunter, wo das schöne mit Blumen erfüllte Thal ist, über das goldene Wölkchen ziehen ... Links sehe ich nichts als Grab und Verwesung ... Vor mir sehe ich nichts als die Welt in ihrer Eitelkeit ... Hinter mir sehe ich Menschen, wie die Löwen und Drachen, sie streiten und kämpfen mit einander ... Ich stehe auf der Spitze dieses Berges, da ist kein Gras, kein Moos ... Um diesen sind noch sieben Berge ... Du, meine Führerin, mit dir will ich gehen, du Heilige! ... Es ist ein Fels, auf dem ich stehe, er hängt ja ... Ha! das ist der Abschnitt, die vier Monate ... Warum sagst du zu mir: ich soll links hinunterschauen? Da ist ja Grab und Tod! .. Rechts lächeln mir die Blumen freundlich zu — aber lieber will ich hin, wo Grab und Tod ist ... Soll ich denn hinunterstürzen unter den Strich? ... Du, führe mich, wohin Du willst ... o banger Traum! ... Führe mich! ... Soll ich denn in den Abgrund stürzen? ... Mächtig bist du, stark genug ... Verstehe ich dich recht oder nicht? ... Muß ich stehen bleiben auf diesem Berge? ... Ja! ich muß stehen bleiben, bis die Stunde da ist, doch bist du bei mir Tag und Nacht ... Bist du nicht bei mir, so falle ich ... O laß mich erwachen aus diesem bangen Traum! ... Laß mich riechen, daß ich erwache — laß mich an diesem riechen, daß ich keine Ahnung habe und es vergesse.“

Es war nun, als würde ihr etwas zum Riechen dargeboten, sie roch, erwachte, und hatte von diesem Traume, gegen die sonstige Weise eines magnetischen Traumes, durchaus keine Erinnerung mehr.

Am 2. Mai, Abends 7 Uhr, verfiel sie in magnetischen Schlaf. Um diese Stunde fielen in ihr jene vier Monate ab und machten einem neuen Cyklus von sieben Sonnenkreisen Raum, von denen sie besonders den ersten fühlte.

„In diesem neuen Kreise,“ sprach sie, „stoße ich ganz unten an der zweiten Linie an und fiel also in den magnetischen Raum dieses Kreises. Aber dieses neue magnetische Leben ist nur ein inneres tiefes Schauen für mich. Ich kann in diesem Kreise wieder hin, wo ich will, bin ich aber tief schlafend (wie kann man es aber doch schlafen nennen!), spreche ich mich nicht aus, wie früher; aber was ich da sah und empfand, geht als wie eine Ahnung mit mir in das wache Leben über, doch wird es

> “I stand on a mountain; to the right I would like to go down, where the beautiful valley filled with flowers is, over which the little golden clouds pass... To the left I see nothing but the grave and decay... Before me I see nothing but the world in its vanity... Behind me I see people, like lions and dragons; they strive and fight with one another... I stand on the peak of this mountain; there is no grass, no moss... Around this one are seven more mountains... You, my guide <note>original: "Führerin." In her trances, the Seeress often spoke to a protective female spirit or "light-guide."</note>, I will go with you, you holy one! ... It is a rock on which I stand; it is hanging... Ha! That is the section, the four months... Why do you say to me: I should look down to the left? There is indeed the grave and death! .. To the right the flowers smile at me friendlily—but I would rather go where the grave and death are... Shall I then plunge down below the line? ... You, lead me wherever You will ... oh, anxious dream! ... Lead me! ... Shall I then plunge into the abyss? ... You are mighty, strong enough ... Do I understand you rightly or not? ... Must I remain standing on this mountain? ... Yes! I must remain standing until the hour is here, yet you are with me day and night ... If you are not with me, I fall ... O let me awaken from this anxious dream! ... Let me smell [something], so that I awaken—let me smell this, so that I have no inkling and forget it.”

It was now as if something were offered to her to smell; she smelled it, awoke, and had—contrary to the usual manner of a <term>magnetic dream<note>A dream experienced during "animal magnetism" or Mesmerism, a 19th-century practice where patients entered trance states believed to facilitate spiritual healing and clairvoyance.</note></term>—absolutely no memory of this dream anymore.

On May 2nd, at 7 o'clock in the evening, she fell into a magnetic sleep. At this hour, those four months <note>Referring to the lost "life-capital" mentioned on the previous page.</note> fell away from her and gave way to a new <term>cycle<note>original: "Cyklus."</note></term> of seven <term>sun-circles<note>In the Seeress's cosmology, time and life-force were visualized as concentric "sun-circles" and "life-circles."</note></term>, of which she felt the first one especially.

“In this new circle,” she spoke, “I strike the second line at the very bottom and thus fell into the magnetic space of this circle. But this new magnetic life is only an inner, deep <term>vision<note>original: "Schauen." This refers to a state of spiritual looking or "seeing" with the internal mind rather than the physical eyes.</note></term> for me. In this circle I can go again where I want; but when I am deep asleep (though how can one still call it sleeping!), I do not express myself as before; but what I saw and felt there carries over into my waking life like a presentiment, yet it will

<summary>The Seeress experiences a vivid, symbolic vision of a mountain surrounded by death and vanity before transitioning into a new seven-year spiritual cycle. This transition marks a shift in her "magnetic life," moving from verbalized trances toward a more internal, intuitive form of spiritual "vision."</summary>

Der Mensch erhält mit der Geburt eine Summe der Kraft, welche, wenn keine Störungen eintreten, sein natürliches Alter bestimmt, aber auch zugleich die Einheit der Zahl, welche die Cyklen seiner Stufenjahre enthält. Dieß gibt denn ein Lebens=kapital, das bis zur vollen Mannbarkeit immer zunimmt, d. h. wo die Einnahme immer größer wird als der Verbrauch. Durch das Mannesalter ist Ersatz und Verbrauch einander gleich, dann aber nimmt das Kapital ab, bis es auf Null gesetzt wird, und dieß ist der natürliche Tod. Die Seherin ist nun gerade in dem Alter, wo Ersatz und Verbrauch sich immer compensiren sollten. Bei ihrem gesteigerten Nervenleben aber, besonders wenn Ge=müthsaffekte hinzukommen, ist der Verlust größer als der Ersatz, und dieß geht vom Lebenskapital hinweg. Alle Jahre fällt zwar ein Sonnenkreis ab, dieß ist aber nur ein Theil von dem Cyklus der sieben Jahre, welcher die Einheit ihrer Zahl bildet.

Die Seherin berechnet vier Monate Verlust, und diese fehlen nun (außer den frühern Verlusten!!) an der Einheit ihres Cyklus. Daher erscheint ihr Sonnenkreis (s. Tab. 4 A und B) wie gebrochen, was sie mit den Worten auszudrücken scheint: „Diese vier Monate hängen ja nur.“ Zwischen dem vollendeten Cyklus und dem Anfang des neuen Cyklus schweben diese vier Monate, welche von dem neuen Sonnenkreis eingeschoben und ergänzt werden sollen.

Die Seherin nennt diesen Zustand ein Eingesperrtseyn, wo sie allein laufen müsse. Sind diese Momente durchlaufen, also bis zum 2. Mai, dann erst kann der neue Cyklus, oder die neue Einheit ihrer Zahl, beginnen. Sie fühlt sich immer noch unter dem gerade ins Centrum gehenden Strich und gibt, was merkwürdig ist, je nach dem Bestand ihrer Nervenkraft, die möglichen Fälle an, die sich für ihr organisches und geistiges Leben ereignen können.

Welcher wird wohl nun eintreten? — eine Frage, die erst der 2. Mai beantworten wird.

> auch da von mir selten ausgesprochen. Der ins Centrum laufende Strich fiel mit den vier Monaten ab, ist nicht mehr auf mir. Hab' ich aber eine heftige Gemüthsbewegung, so springt der von diesen neuen sieben Kreisen ins Centrum laufende Strich auf mich. Mein Körperliches bleibt, wie es ist, mein Körper ist lebendig todt, aber meine Seele ruhiger und freier, wie noch nie. Auf meinen Körper darf gar keine Rücksicht mehr genommen werden, kein Mensch darf sich darum eine Sorge machen, ich denke gar nicht mehr an dieses zerrissene Kleid und empfehle nur, o Vater, in deine Hände meinen Geist!"

->Das war die Vorahnung ihres baldigen Todes!<-

Ihre sonst so ängstliche Sorge um ihren Körper fiel nun auch ganz hinweg. Zwar war dieser noch nicht fähig, organische Kraft aus sich selbst zu schöpfen, und ihr Zustand blieb, wie er es schon lange war, ein ins wache Leben getretener magnetischer; aber ihr Wesen hatte sich seit ihrem Aufenthalt hier günstig verändert, sie war hier mehr zu einer innern Klarheit und Ruhe gekommen, ihr Geist hatte hier oft, auch durch den Umgang mit manchen würdigen Menschen, Aufrichtung und Erheiterung gefunden, die in ihrem Innern fortwirkten, lag es auch nicht in ihrer Freunde Macht, Vieles, das auf ihren Körper nachtheilig in dieser Zeit einfließen mußte (wie z. At birth, a human being receives a sum of force which—provided no disruptions occur—determines their natural age, but also simultaneously the unit of the number that contains the cycles of their <term>graduated years<note>original: "Stufenjahre." These are significant years in a person's life, often occurring in seven-year intervals, believed in various esoteric traditions to mark major physical and spiritual transitions.</note></term>. This constitutes a <term>life-capital<note>original: "Lebenskapital." A metaphor for the total store of vital energy a person possesses.</note></term> that increases until full maturity; that is, the stage where "income" is always greater than "expenditure." During the prime of life, restoration and consumption are equal to one another, but thereafter the capital decreases until it is set to zero, which is natural death. The Seeress is now exactly at the age where restoration and consumption should always <term>compensate<note>original: "compensiren." To balance or offset.</note></term> for each other. However, due to her heightened <term>nerve-life<note>original: "Nervenleben." In 19th-century medicine, the "nerves" were often seen as the conductors of a semi-physical, semi-spiritual fluid or force.</note></term>, especially when emotional disturbances are added, the loss is greater than the restoration, and this is deducted from her life-capital. Every year, a <term>sun-circle<note>In her visions, the Seeress saw time as a series of concentric circles; a "sun-circle" represented a single year.</note></term> falls away, but this is only one part of the seven-year cycle that forms the unit of her number.

The Seeress calculates a loss of four months, and these are now missing (aside from earlier losses!!) from the unit of her cycle. Therefore, her sun-circle (see Table 4 A and B) appears as if broken, which she seems to express with the words: "These four months are just hanging." These four months hover between the completed cycle and the beginning of the new cycle, and they are meant to be inserted and completed by the new sun-circle.

The Seeress calls this state a "being locked in," where she must run alone. Only when these moments have been traversed—that is, by the 2nd of May—can the new cycle, or the new unit of her number, begin. She still feels herself beneath the line that goes straight into the center and, remarkably, depending on the state of her <term>nerve-force<note>original: "Nervenkraft." The vital energy that sustains both physical health and clairvoyant abilities.</note></term>, she indicates the possible outcomes that could occur for her organic and spiritual life.

Which one will actually occur? — a question that only the 2nd of May will answer.

A dream occurring while in a state of "animal magnetism" or trance, believed to be prophetic or deeply meaningful.</note></term> of the Seeress; she spoke it aloud as usual, but it was only imperfectly transcribed:

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 57, which explored how the stomach functions as a site of internal fermentation and how its vapors reveal the state of digestion. It transitions here from the human stomach to the chemical distillation of grain, drawing a parallel between biological and laboratory processes.</meta>

(58)

Since the stomach is the *residence* and seat of the spiritual power <note>original: *geistlichen Krafft*; the vital force or "spirit" believed to animate the body and govern nutrition</note> to nourish man / and to impart new blood <note>original: *Geblüth*; the body's entire blood supply</note> to the heart / as well as new power of imagination <note>original: *Einbildungs macht*; the mental faculty of thought and visualization</note> to the brain / and new reproductive fluid <note>original: *Zeugungs Safft*; the "vital seeds" or procreative juices</note> to the seminal vessels / one can thus easily judge the changes that occur in a person almost daily / regarding both their healthy and sick states. *Let the wise man take up his thoughts upon this part with every edge of his genius.* <note>original Latin: *Sapiens omni acie ingenii suas hanc partem Cogitationes suscipiat.*</note>

Now the *distillation* of the grain itself shall follow / which will bring such things to light / as reason and the senses would never have sought in the grains of the corn. Accordingly, take the above-mentioned *fermented* or leavened mass / and place it in a bladder <note>original: *Blase*; in early chemistry, this refers to the copper boiling vessel or the body of the still</note> greased on the inside with lard <note>original: *Speck*; literally bacon or fat, used here to prevent the mash from sticking and burning</note> / in order to prevent any scorched smell <note>original: *Brenzlichten Geruch*; the acrid, burnt odor of organic material overheated in a still</note> / place it in a suitable furnace / make a fire under the bladder / and stir the mass therein with a mixing stick for as long as it takes / until it becomes warm / then place a helmet or cap <note>original: *Helm* or *Huth*; the alembic head or "still-head" where the vapors collect</note> on top / whose tubes [pass] through a barrel full of cold water / and further into a receiver— <note>original: *Vorlage*; the vessel at the end of the distillation apparatus that collects the condensed spirit. The text breaks here because "Vorlage" is the catchword for the next page.</note>

<summary>This page concludes the analogy between the human stomach and chemical vessels, then provides practical instructions for distilling grain, including how to prevent a burnt smell by greasing the still.</summary>
<keywords>digestion, vital force, distillation, grain spirit, alchemy, laboratory apparatus, fermentation, anatomy of the stomach</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical discussion regarding the relationship between Spirit and Matter, completing the word "Matter" from the previous page's final sentence.</meta>

<page-num>314</page-num>
# The 44th Letter.

...matter <note>completing the word "Matter" from the previous page</note> are two truly distinct things, indeed two complete substances, which are nevertheless homogeneous <note>of the same nature or kind</note> according to the homogeneity of the **originating principle** <note>original: *principii principiantis*; the creative source from which all principles emerge</note>. Thus, they are from a single root, which among true philosophers is considered the same thing.

You will perhaps think to yourself that all **mixtures** <note>original: *mixta*; physical substances composed of different elements</note>, however much they differ in form and nature, are homogeneous according to the homogeneity of the **principle**, because the matter which is subject to their form is homogeneous with the aforementioned **Universal Spirit** <note>the fundamental life-force believed to permeate the cosmos</note> according to the preceding teaching. Thus, they are of one and the same root, and each can be taken as the matter for the **multiplication** <note>the alchemical process of increasing the power or quantity of a substance, typically the Philosopher's Stone</note> of any other. If this holds true among mixed things which differ in form and number, it will much more hold true within the natural parts of every mixed thing—insofar as it is a **mixture** <note>original: *mixtum*</note>—namely, in its **Mercury**, **Salt**, and **Sulfur**. This is because these parts share the same material beginning with their whole, both in number and form. This objection is certainly strong, and its resolution is hardly to be found expressed so specifically anywhere else; now, we wish for you to hear it here.

<summary>This page explores the alchemical theory that Spirit and Matter share a single "originating principle," leading to a discussion on why different substances can be seen as fundamentally homogeneous. The author raises a significant philosophical objection regarding whether all mixtures can be used to multiply one another since they all stem from the same root of Mercury, Salt, and Sulfur.</summary>

<keywords>Universal Spirit, Matter, homogeneity, originating principle, mixtures, multiplication, Mercury, Salt, Sulfur, alchemical theory</keywords>

## Essay on Spirit-Seeing

### and what is connected with it.

...the positive current goes through these fluids, from the zinc to the copper, and then outside of them, at the electrode, back from the copper to the zinc. Analogous to this, the positive current of the **life force** <note>original: "Lebenskraft." A 19th-century concept of a vital energy that animates living beings, often associated with electricity or magnetism.</note>—acting as the **Will** <term>For Schopenhauer, the "Will" is the fundamental, blind force that underlies all reality; here, he treats the magnetizer's focused intent as a physical force.</term> of the **magnetizer** <note>A practitioner of "animal magnetism" or Mesmerism, who believed they could heal or influence others by directing a "magnetic fluid" through their hands.</note>—would go from his brain to that of the **somnambulist** <note>A person in a deep, magnetically induced trance who was often believed to possess clairvoyant powers.</note>, dominating it and driving back her own life force (which produces consciousness in the brain) to the **sympathetic nerve** <note>The sympathetic nervous system, which Schopenhauer and his contemporaries viewed as a secondary "abdominal brain" that became the seat of consciousness during a trance.</note>, that is, the **region of the stomach** <gloss>the epigastrium</gloss>, her negative pole. Then, however, that same current would go further from here back into the magnetizer, to his positive pole, his brain, where it encounters his thoughts and sensations, which the somnambulist then becomes a participant in. These are, of course, very daring assumptions: but with things so entirely unexplained as those which are our problem here, any hypothesis that leads to some understanding—even if only schematic or analogical—is permissible.

The exceedingly miraculous—and therefore, until it was confirmed by the agreement of hundreds of the most credible testimonies, absolutely unbelievable—phenomenon of **somnambulist clairvoyance**, in which what is hidden, absent, distant, or even still slumbering in the womb of the future lies open, loses at least its absolute incomprehensibility if we consider well that, as I have so often said, the objective world is a mere **brain-phenomenon**. For it is the order and lawfulness of the world based on **space, time, and causality** (as brain functions) which is, to a certain degree, abolished in somnambulist clairvoyance. Namely, as a result of the **Kantian doctrine** <note>The philosophy of Immanuel Kant, who argued that space and time are not properties of the world itself, but rather "filters" or "forms" through which the human mind perceives reality.</note> of the **ideality of space and time**, we understand that the **thing-in-itself** <term>The "Ding an sich"—reality as it exists independently of our perception.</term>—the only truly real thing in all appearances—is free from those two forms of the intellect and knows no difference between near and far, or between present, past, and future. Therefore, the separations based on those **forms of intuition** <note>original: "Anschauungsformen." The mental frameworks (space and time) we use to organize our sensory input.</note> do not prove to be absolute; instead, for the mode of knowledge in question, which is essentially changed by the transformation of its organ, they no longer present any insurmountable barriers. If, on the contrary, time and space were absolutely real and belonged to the essence-in-itself of things, then that seers'—

<meta>This page continues Schopenhauer’s physiological explanation of animal magnetism, specifically how the "life force" or "nerve force" is shifted from the brain (the conscious pole) to the ganglionic system (the unconscious pole) during a magnetic trance. The previous page established that the magnetizer's "brain pole" repels the patient's, pushing their consciousness down into the organic, vegetative centers of the body.</meta>

### and what is connected with it.

...in the magnetic sleep of everyone;—comparable to the lotus, which sinks into the flood at evening. This also corresponds to the fact that when the conductors of the **tub** <note>original: "Baquet." A vat filled with water and iron filings used in Mesmerism to "concentrate" magnetic fluid for patients to hold onto.</note> were once applied to the head instead of the pit of the stomach, violent congestion and headache were the result (Rieser, *Tellurism*, 1st ed., Vol. 1, p. 439). 

That in the **sidereal tub** <note>original: "siderischen Baquet." A version of the Mesmeric tub that used metals and physical substances to influence patients without the presence of a "magnetizer" to charge them.</note>, bare, unmagnetized metals exert the same force seems to be related to the fact that metal is the simplest, most original, and lowest stage of the **objectification of the Will** <term>In Schopenhauer’s philosophy, "Will" is the fundamental force of the universe, and everything—from rocks to humans—is a physical "objectification" or manifestation of that Will at different levels of complexity.</term>. Consequently, metal is the polar opposite of the brain, which represents the highest development of this objectification, and is thus the thing most distant from it; furthermore, metal presents the greatest mass in the smallest space. It therefore recalls the Will to its original state and is related to the **ganglionic system** <note>The network of nerves (sympathetic nervous system) that controls involuntary functions like digestion and heartbeat.</note>, just as light is conversely related to the brain. This is why **somnambulists** <note>Individuals in a deep state of magnetic or hypnotic trance.</note> dread the contact of metals with the organs of the conscious pole [the head]. The ability of those specifically sensitive to "feel" metal and water [dowsing] also finds its explanation here. 

If, in the case of the ordinary magnetized tub, the active force is the combined ganglionic systems of all the patients gathered around it—who, with united strength, pull down the brain poles—this also provides a guide for explaining the "contagion" of somnambulism in general. It also explains the related transmission of the active **second sight** <note>original: "zweites Gesicht." Clairvoyance or the ability to perceive things hidden in time or space.</note> through contact between those so gifted, and the transmission—and thus the shared experience—of visions in general.

If, however, one were to allow a still bolder application of the above hypothesis—which is based on the laws of polarity regarding the process of active **magnetizing** <note>The practice of "animal magnetism" (Mesmerism), where a vital fluid or force was thought to be transferred from the healer to the patient.</note>—it could be derived (if only schematically) how, in the higher degrees of somnambulism, the **rapport** <note>The special psychological and physical "link" established between the magnetizer and the subject.</note> can go so far that the somnambulist shares in all the thoughts, knowledge, languages, and even all the sensory perceptions of the magnetizer. She is, in effect, present in his brain, while his Will has a direct influence on her and dominates her so completely that he can hold her fast in a spell. <summary>Schopenhauer uses a polar model of the nervous system to explain Mesmeric phenomena, suggesting that metals attract the "unconscious" ganglionic system and repel the "conscious" brain, leading to shared visions and the deep "rapport" of the hypnotic state.</summary>

§ 192. The animal sphere can also act in the reverse ratio, through the apparatus of semi-conduction, upon the vegetative, and become determining for it.

Thus, for example, the brain acts continuously as a stimulant upon the entire vegetative sphere according to the measure of its state of activity, and produces an activity in it, which it then takes back into itself again as a general feeling. The pleasant feeling that the expanded sphere of our mental activity excites in us arises probably only through the irritation of the excited brain, which is refracted back as a general feeling. Since, furthermore, the vital force within the animal sphere is subject to the will (§ 180), it will also be able to be accumulated against the apparatus of semi-conduction when the former is of sufficient strength, where a jumping over and influencing of the vegetative sphere then easily becomes possible.

As proof that the strong will can intervene in the actions of vegetative life and determine its activity, more or less, I do not mention those examples where individual people had the circulation of the blood in their control, could move the iris at will <note>a)</note>, and the like, for these are peculiarities that can have their basis in the individual organization (as, for example, in the latter case in a lack of the ocular ganglion), but I refer merely to that which has long been known and only recently expressed again by Kant

Or <term>Mencius</term> a dit: l'étude doit délivrer le cœur, le conserver, l'alimenter, afin qu'il puisse servir le ciel. Que les étudiants notent cela !... Il en est de la méditation, comme d'une graine qui contient une force vitale, un germe de développement. Cultivée, elle déploiera sa vertu, se développera et produira. Ainsi en sera-t-il de l'homme qui médite. Si on ne soigne pas la graine, elle ne donnera rien. Celui qui ne progresse pas, doit s'en prendre à lui-même. Il n'a pas fumé, biné, arrosé... Des trois choses, méditation, résolution, exécution, la méditation est la première, car elle produit la résolution, laquelle produit l'exécution.

<term>Mencius</term> a dit que, pour garder son cœur en bon état, il fallait diminuer ses désirs le plus possible. Cela revient à dire, qu'il faut le bien garder. Le délivrer autant que possible de toute affection déréglée... <term>Confucius</term> a parfaitement défini ce en quoi doit consister la maîtrise de soi. Ne rien regarder, écouter, dire; ne faire aucun mouvement, qui ne convienne. Cette réserve dans les communications avec l'extérieur, préserve l'intérieur. Sage est celui qui l'observe !

Pour ce qui est des mauvaises pensées qui s'élèvent dans le cœur, les plus considérables sont faciles à reconnaître et à réprimer. Mais que faire contre ces mouvements innombrables qui sont presque imperceptibles?.. Il n'y a qu'à ne pas les suivre, quand on les a remarqués. Tel un homme assis. Il veut rester assis. Ses jambes voudraient marcher. Quoique les jambes lui démangent ainsi, il reste assis, et ne marchera que quand il voudra marcher.

Jadis 趙叔平 <term>Tchao chou-p'ing</term> usa du moyen que voici. Il mit des fèves blanches dans un vase, des fèves noires dans un autre vase; entre les deux, il mit un vase vide. Chaque fois que dans son cœur une bonne pensée bougeait, il prenait une fève blanche et la jetait dans le vase du milieu. Chaque fois qu'une mauvaise pensée bougeait, il prenait une fève noire et la jetait dans le vase du milieu. La nuit venue, il vidait ce vase, comptait les fèves noires ou blanches, et notait ainsi le nombre de ses pensées bonnes ou mauvaises. Au début, les fèves noires étaient nombreuses, et les blanches rares. Avec le temps, peu à peu, les deux sortes vinrent à se balancer. A la longue, les blanches l'emportèrent sur les noires. Enfin il n'y eut plus que des fèves blanches, et cela dura. Son cœur était purifié, réduit à la simplicité, à l'unité, au bien pur sans mélange de mal.

Il en est qui prient les <term>koei</term> et les <term>chenn</term>, pour leur demander du bonheur. Cela est-il raisonnable? Cela peut-il avoir quelque résultat?.. Au bien et au mal de l'homme, répondent le bonheur et le malheur du ciel. La voie du ciel, c'est de rendre heureux les bons, et de rendre malheureux les méchants. Les <term>koei</term> et les <term>chenn</term> ne sauraient rien faire contre cette voie du ciel. Chacun est coupable du mal qu'il a fait. On obtient par les bonnes œuvres d'être exempté des fléaux célestes..... Mais n'est-ce pas un fait que certains, qui n'ont fait que du bien, ont péri misérablement; et que certains, qui ont fait beaucoup de mal, ont été comblés de biens?.. Le fait est vrai. C'est là l'effet du hasard, ce qu'on appelle la chance. La chance est destin pur. Cela ne devrait pas être, mais c'est le lot. Personne n'échappe à son destin, personne ne peut changer son lot.
