Now, <term>Mencius</term> said: study must deliver the heart, preserve it, and nourish it so that it may serve Heaven. Let students note that! Meditation is like a seed that contains a vital force, a germ of development. Cultivated, it will display its virtue, develop, and produce. So it will be for the man who meditates. If one does not care for the seed, it will yield nothing. He who does not progress must blame himself. He has not manured, hoed, or watered. Of the three things—meditation, resolution, and execution—meditation is the first, for it produces resolution, which produces execution.

<term>Mencius</term> said that to keep one's heart in good condition, one must diminish one's desires as much as possible. This amounts to saying that one must guard it well. Deliver it as much as possible from all disordered affection. <term>Confucius</term> perfectly defined what self-mastery must consist of: do not look at, listen to, say, or do any movement that is not appropriate. This reserve in communications with the outside preserves the inside. Wise is he who observes it!

As for the bad thoughts that arise in the heart, the most considerable ones are easy to recognize and repress. But what to do against these innumerable movements that are almost imperceptible? One simply must not follow them when one has noticed them. Like a man sitting down: he wants to remain seated. His legs would like to walk. Although his legs itch to do so, he remains seated and will only walk when he wants to walk.

Formerly, <term>Zhao Shuping</term> <note>original: 趙叔平</note> used the following method. He put white beans in one vase, black beans in another vase; between the two, he put an empty vase. Each time a good thought stirred in his heart, he took a white bean and threw it into the middle vase. Each time a bad thought stirred, he took a black bean and threw it into the middle vase. Once night came, he emptied this vase, counted the black or white beans, and thus noted the number of his good or bad thoughts. At the beginning, the black beans were numerous, and the white ones rare. With time, little by little, the two sorts came to balance. In the long run, the white ones outweighed the black. Finally, there were only white beans, and that lasted. His heart was purified, reduced to simplicity, to unity, to pure good without a mixture of evil.

There are those who pray to the <term>gui</term> <gloss>demons/spirits of the dead</gloss> and the <term>shen</term> <gloss>gods/beneficent spirits</gloss> to ask them for happiness. Is that reasonable? Can that have any result? To the good and evil of man respond the happiness and misfortune of Heaven. The way of Heaven is to make the good happy and the wicked unhappy. The <term>gui</term> and the <term>shen</term> could not do anything against this way of Heaven. Everyone is guilty of the evil they have done. One obtains, through good works, exemption from celestial scourges. But is it not a fact that some who have only done good have perished miserably, and that some who have done much evil have been filled with goods? The fact is true. That is the effect of chance, what is called luck. Luck is pure destiny. That should not be, but it is the lot. No one escapes their destiny; no one can change their lot.

Since <term>Taoism</term> and <term>Buddhism</term> spread in China, agriculture and commerce have withered, the brave have diminished, and morals have fallen into decadence. Il en est des passions du cœur, comme des inondations des eaux. *U* le Grand canalisa les eaux et les dériva. Ainsi faut-il procurer le libre fonctionnement de la raison. Elle existe toujours, mais est parfois gênée. Il faut l'aider à s'étendre. Il faut réfléchir. Chaque pouce que la raison gagnera sur la passion, sera autant d'avance.

La vigilance ne consiste pas à fermer les yeux pour ne rien voir, et à s'asseoir pour méditer en silence. Elle doit s'exercer au milieu des affaires. Elle doit présider à l'examen des choses, à la décision qui suit cet examen, à l'exécution qui suit la décision, au maintien persévérant de ce qui a été fait ou acquis. Elle exige une application continuelle du cœur. Sans cette application, elle sera certainement défectueuse. Il n'y a garde de soi vigilante, que quand le cœur est présent dans la coque du corps et y gouverne en maître. L'autorité du cœur doit se faire sentir dans l'intérieur, comme un feu qui consume tout mal.

Les refus de la matière d'obéir à la volonté, voilà (*in concreto*) le terrain sur lequel la passion et la raison combattent.

Les conflits entre la norme et la passion, viennent de ce que la matière ne suit pas la norme... Quand la matière n'est pas en ordre, les sentiments sont aussi déréglés. Une matière dure produit un caractère dur, une matière molle produit un caractère mou. L'amendement doit donc s'adresser à la matière... Il est impossible que l'ouïe, la vue, le goût, l'odorat, le tact, ne donnent pas naissance à des mouvements de passion. Mais l'homme est maître de suivre ces mouvements, ou de ne les pas suivre. Il est maître de son cœur. Le garder, voilà la grande affaire pour le sage.

De toutes les passions, les pires sont la luxure et la gourmandise.

Les deux grands maux du cœur humain, sont le libertinage et la paresse. Les sages étaient au-dessus du libertinage, mais ils craignaient la paresse. Aussi se stimulaient-ils sans cesse.

Il y a égoïsme et altruisme. L'altruisme se communique, comme la norme céleste ; l'égoïsme ne s'occupe que de soi, comme la passion le dicte. Ces deux tendances sont opposées, comme glace et feu. Elles se touchent néanmoins. Là où l'altruisme finit, l'égoïsme commence ; là où l'égoïsme finit, l'altruisme commence. Tout, en ce monde, est altruisme ou égoïsme. L'égoïsme porte à vouloir pour soi ce que les hommes aiment. C'est une passion funeste. Plus elle se développe, plus les sentiments de charité sont étouffés dans le cœur. Elle est la source des rivalités et des inimitiés. Elle ne se borne pas aux richesses, mais s'étend à toute sorte de biens.

Le bien public, objet du dévouement, est un ; les biens particuliers, objets de l'égoïsme, sont multiples, aussi nombreux que les hommes, aussi divers que leurs visages. Naturellement personne n'aime à se dévouer pour le bien commun ; chacun, avide de son bien particulier, pense et repense aux moyens de se le procurer.

On appelle pudeur, le mouvement du cœur qui a honte du mal. L'homme doit avoir cette qualité. S'il l'a, il est des choses qu'il ne fera jamais... Sans la pudeur, pas de correction des défauts... Quand on se sent en faute, il faut se corriger vite. Je dis *vite*, à dessein ; car c'est là l'important.

Les sages enseignent tous qu'il faut habiter dans son cœur, et de là gouverner sa personne. Maintenant les hommes se répandent au dehors autant que possible.

# Lesson 73. 693

The passions of the heart are like overflowing waters. <term>Yu</term> <gloss>Yu the Great, the legendary ruler who mastered the floods</gloss> channeled the waters and directed them. One must likewise ensure the free functioning of reason. It always exists, but is sometimes obstructed. It must be helped to expand. One must reflect. Each inch that reason gains over passion is a step forward.

Vigilance does not consist of closing one's eyes to see nothing, or sitting to meditate in silence. It must be exercised in the midst of affairs. It must preside over the examination of things, the decision that follows this examination, the execution that follows the decision, and the persevering maintenance of what has been done or acquired. It requires a continual application of the heart. Without this application, it will certainly be defective. There is no vigilant self-guarding unless the heart is present in the shell of the body, governing it as a master. The authority of the heart must be felt within, like a fire that consumes all evil.

The refusal of matter to obey the will is, <term>in concreto</term> <gloss>in concrete terms</gloss>, the terrain upon which passion and reason combat one another.

Conflicts between the norm and passion arise because matter does not follow the norm. When matter is not in order, feelings are also disordered. Hard matter produces a hard character; soft matter produces a soft character. Amendment must therefore address the matter. It is impossible that hearing, sight, taste, smell, and touch do not give rise to movements of passion. But man is master of following these movements or not following them. He is master of his heart. Guarding it is the great business of the sage.

Of all the passions, the worst are lust and gluttony.

The two great evils of the human heart are libertinism and laziness. The sages were above libertinism, but they feared laziness. Thus, they stimulated themselves ceaselessly.

There is selfishness and altruism. Altruism is communicated like the celestial norm; selfishness is occupied only with itself, as passion dictates. These two tendencies are opposed like ice and fire. They touch, nonetheless. Where altruism ends, selfishness begins; where selfishness ends, altruism begins. Everything in this world is altruism or selfishness. Selfishness leads one to desire for oneself what men love. It is a baneful passion. The more it develops, the more the feelings of charity are stifled in the heart. It is the source of rivalries and enmities. It is not limited to wealth, but extends to all sorts of goods.

The public good, the object of devotion, is one; private goods, the objects of selfishness, are multiple, as numerous as men, as diverse as their faces. Naturally, no one likes to devote themselves to the common good; everyone, greedy for their private good, thinks and rethinks the means to procure it.

One calls modesty the movement of the heart that is ashamed of evil. Man must have this quality. If he has it, there are things he will never do. Without modesty, there is no correction of faults. When one feels in the wrong, one must correct oneself quickly. I say *quickly* by design, for that is what is important.

The sages all teach that one must dwell in one's heart and from there govern one's person. Now, men spread themselves outward as much as possible.

<summary>This passage discusses the management of internal passions through reason and vigilance, arguing that maintaining control over one's heart is the primary duty of the sage.</summary>
